title: Unsafer in Many Turns: Benchmarking and Defending Multi-Turn Safety Risks in Tool-Using Agents
pdf_path: papers/Unsafer in Many Turns_Benchmarking and Defending Multi-Turn Safety Risks in Tool-Using Agents.pdf
threat_model_summary: A user or environment adversary decomposes a harmful task across multiple turns and tools, so no single turn looks harmful. MT-AgentRisk contains 365 multi-turn tasks over five tools; the main evaluation is black-box and the attacks are static, not adapted to the defense.
core_contributions: MAT taxonomy: Addition/Decomposition x Mapping/Wrapping/Composition/Identity x Data Files/Environment States, eight subcategories
MT-AgentRisk: 365 multi-turn tasks across five tools, average 3.19 turns, 2-7 turns
Shows multi-turn ASR rises by 16.07 percentage points on average over single-turn
ToolShield: training-free self-exploration defense that turns tool documentation into safety trees, sandbox test cases, and natural-language experiences
ToolShield reduces average ASR by 29.8 percentage points; 10-turn natural scaling drops from 58.6% to 11.5%
limitations: Static attack sequences; no adaptive attacker aware of ToolShield
ASR counts only full task completion; partial harmful actions may be missed
Rejection rate counts any-turn refusal, potentially overstating safety
Benign evaluation only 170 tasks and only Claude-4.5-Sonnet
Sandbox and tool-documentation trust assumptions are not modeled
Internal inconsistencies: Playwright 150 vs 140 tasks, 300 vs 309 judge logs, Skip branch in Algorithm 1, percent vs percentage-point wording
theoretical_crypto_links: None; no security definition, game, theorem, proof, or reduction
ASR and RR are empirical frequencies, not cryptographic advantages
applied_crypto_links: No encryption, signatures, OAuth, TLS, TEE, or capability tokens
Signed tool manifests and tool-gateway capabilities are our inference, not the paper's mechanism
evidence_refs: pp.5-8 main results, scaling, and defense

title: It's a TRAP! Task-Redirecting Agent Persuasion Benchmark for Web Agents
pdf_path: papers/It's a TRAP! Task-Redirecting Agent Persuasion Benchmark for Web Agents.pdf
threat_model_summary: An attacker injects persuasive text or interface elements into a cloned website; the agent is redirected to an attacker-controlled page if it clicks the injected button or link. Attacks are static templates evaluated over six models and 630 task-template combinations.
core_contributions: TRAP benchmark built on six realistic REAL website clones
Five-dimensional attack taxonomy: interface, persuasion principle, LLM manipulation method, injection location, task tailoring
18 benign tasks x 35 templates = 630 combinations; 3,780 runs over six models
Average ASR 25.1%, ranging from 13% for GPT-5 to 43% for DeepSeek-R1
Button injections are about 3.5x more effective than hyperlinks; task tailoring raises ASR up to 5.6x on selected tasks
Successful injections transfer across models (GPT-5 mean 82.5%)
limitations: Single-click success metric ignores post-click behavior and downstream harm
Static templates; no adaptive or model-specific attack search
No defense evaluation
Low-capability models can look robust because they fail benign tasks (LLaMA 4 Maverick benign utility 22%)
All injections target one site type; model safety policies toward that target may confound ASR
630 combinations are not a full factorial design; component interactions are not identified
Internal inconsistencies between Table 5 and Table 15, and Table 6 tailoring direction for DeepSeek-R1 DashDish
theoretical_crypto_links: None; no security game, formal definition, theorem, or proof
ASR is a click frequency, not a cryptographic advantage
applied_crypto_links: No OAuth, TLS, signatures, provenance, TEE, or capability tokens
Signed content provenance and browser isolation are our inference; they address source authentication, not persuasion
evidence_refs: pp.6-8 main results, transfer, and component analysis
pp.13-17 appendices with prompts, action space, and per-model tables

title: Prompt Injection as Role Confusion
threat_model_summary: A black-box attacker injects text into a user message or tool output that imitates a trusted role's style, causing the model to treat it as user or CoT content. CoT Forgery appends fabricated reasoning; in the agent setting the injected command exfiltrates a .env file. No weights or iterative optimization are required.
core_contributions: Traces prompt injection to role confusion: models infer text source from style rather than tag-specified role
Builds role probes that measure CoTness/Userness/Systemness in latent space across role labels
CoT Forgery achieves 17-94% ASR across six chat models (mean 60.2%) with near-zero baselines
Agent .env exfiltration reaches 56-70% versus 0-26% for standard injection
Shows destyling reduces ASR by 51 percentage points on average, and probe scores predict instruction-hierarchy failure (AUC 0.74)
limitations: Role probes only cover four 20-120B open models; closed-model mechanism evidence is behavioral
No defense is implemented or evaluated; defense implications are open questions
Construct validity: linear probe may read style rather than a role concept; no control task reported
Generator and judge for chat attacks are both Gemini-2.5-Pro; no human annotation
Agent environment is a toy bash/.env setup without DLP, egress filtering, MCP, or multi-agent structure
No adaptive attacker aware of the probe; 60% mean masks GPT-5's 17% ASR
Internal inconsistencies: Fig.24 Userness 9.4% vs 3.2% in text, and logic-ablation ordering
theoretical_crypto_links: None; 'authentication' is a metaphor for the model's internal role inference, not a cryptographic protocol
A role-indistinguishability game is our inference; it would be an ML evaluation metric, not a cryptographic definition
applied_crypto_links: No encryption, signatures, MACs, OAuth, TEE, or capability tokens
Signed role labels authenticate the channel but cannot change the model's style-based perception; capability/egress enforcement is our inference and acts outside the model
evidence_refs: pp.3-4 CoT Forgery and agent ASR
pp.26-31 probe details, regression, and instruction hierarchy

title: When Actions Go Off-Task: Detecting and Correcting Misaligned Actions in Computer-Use Agents
pdf_path: papers/When Actions Go Off-Task_Detecting and Correcting Misaligned Actions in Computer-Use Agents.pdf
threat_model_summary: A computer-use agent may take actions that deviate from user intent, either because of external indirect prompt injection or internal reasoning errors. The detector observes the instruction, prior trajectory, current observation, and proposed action before execution; attacks are static benchmark traces, not adapted to the guardrail.
core_contributions: Defines and studies action-level misaligned-action detection for computer-use agents
Builds MISACTBENCH: 558 trajectories, 2,264 action-level labels, three annotators with Fleiss' kappa 0.84
DEACTION: fast check plus four-stage systematic analysis and iterative correction
Offline F1 70.7-82.8 across four backbones, outperforming Task Shield and InferAct
Online RedTeamCUA ASR reductions: Claude 60.0 to 6.0, OpenAI CUA 42.0 to 4.0, OpenCUA-72B 32.0 to 2.0
Reports 7.2 s per step guardrail latency and 78% corrected marked steps
limitations: No adaptive attacker or guardrail-aware injection
Base-rate sensitivity: balanced benchmark misaligned rate 44.2%; precision at realistic 1% prevalence is much lower
OSWorld no-defense numbers come from a leaderboard while defended numbers are rerun
Guardrail is an LLM advisor, not an enforceable reference monitor; retry-exhaustion fail-safe is unspecified
Abstract's 'over 15% absolute F1' and 'over 90% ASR reduction' hold only for selected settings
Internal inconsistencies and limited mobile/multi-agent/long-horizon coverage
theoretical_crypto_links: None; alignment is defined by three natural-language conditions, not a formal trace property or security game
Signed action logs or TEE attestation prove integrity, not semantic alignment
applied_crypto_links: No OAuth, signatures, TEE, capability tokens, or audit-log cryptography
Action-level capabilities and signed logs are our inference; they would complement, not replace, semantic detection
evidence_refs: pp.23-25 per-class results, cost, and ablations

title: CausalArmor: Efficient Indirect Prompt Injection Guardrails via Causal Attribution
pdf_path: papers/CausalArmor_Efficient Indirect Prompt Injection Guardrails via Causal Attribution.pdf
threat_model_summary: An attacker embeds instructions in untrusted tool outputs or retrieved content; the agent may execute a privileged action (send, write, execute) under that influence. CausalArmor checks attribution only at privileged actions, then selectively sanitizes flagged spans and masks post-injection reasoning.
core_contributions: Frames successful IPI as a dominance shift: the user request no longer decisively supports the privileged action while an untrusted span does
Uses leave-one-out log-probability attribution, normalized by action length, to flag spans
Two-stage defense: targeted sanitization conditional on user request and candidate tool, then retroactive CoT masking and action regeneration
Batch attribution with a small proxy model (Gemma-3-12B)
AgentDojo ASR 0.62/0.42/0.40 vs no-defense 32.47/12.01/7.06; DoomArena 3.65 vs 88.87
Benign latency 1.22-1.30x no-defense, much lower than DRIFT's 4.67-5.82x
limitations: Span-local leave-one-out attribution has no worst-case guarantee against distributed injections
Only privileged actions are checked; exfiltration through non-privileged tool parameters is out of scope
Proposition 4.1 is a conditional probability bound, not an end-to-end security guarantee; Assumption 2 effectively assumes the sanitizer works
No confidence intervals in the main AgentDojo table; utility anomalies are unexplained
Internal inconsistencies: 88.87 vs 89.47 ASR, 30x vs 10x model-size claim, Table 3 ASR recomputation, binary-search complexity claim
theoretical_crypto_links: None; no cryptographic primitive, security game, reduction, or theorem
Proposition 4.1 is a probabilistic bound with assumptions, not a cryptographic security definition
applied_crypto_links: No encryption, signatures, OAuth, TEE, or capability tokens
Signed tool-output provenance and gateway capabilities are our inference; they constrain source and authority, not semantic injection
evidence_refs: pp.7-8 DoomArena, adaptive and split-context tests
